reference_items.subject: Mathematics
reference_items.stem:
[Image: a stack of square boxes in the corner of a room.]

Ann stacks these boxes in the corner of the room. All the boxes are the same size.
How many boxes does she use?
reference_items.figure_description:
An isometric drawing shows a stack of identical cube-shaped boxes resting in the corner of a room. Three line segments represent the room's edges meeting at the corner behind the stack: a vertical line extends straight up from the top-back corner of the stack, a line extends down and to the left from the bottom-left of the stack along the floor, and a line extends to the right from the bottom-right of the stack along the floor.

The stack rests on the floor against both walls. The base layer is completely filled, measuring 3 cubes deep along the left wall and 4 cubes wide along the back wall (a 3 by 4 grid of cubes).

A second layer of cubes is stacked on top against the corner in a stepped pattern:
- Along the back wall (row 1, closest to the back wall), the first 3 columns from the left are 2 cubes high, and the 4th column is 1 cube high.
- In the middle row (row 2), the first 2 columns from the left are 2 cubes high, and the remaining 2 columns are 1 cube high.
- In the front row (row 3), the first column on the left is 2 cubes high, and the remaining 3 columns are 1 cube high.
reference_items.calibration: Concurrent calibration of the TIMSS 2007 and 2011 fourth-grade mathematics data.

reference_items.subject: Mathematics
reference_items.stem:
[Image: six pieces of cardboard with length of the sides labeled in cm. Two of the pieces are square shaped with each side measured at 1 cm. Four of the pieces are rectangular shaped with two sides measured at 1 cm and two other sides measured at 2 cm.]

Susan has the 6 pieces of cardboard shown above. Which of the following shapes could Susan make using all 6 of these pieces without cutting them?
reference_items.figure_description:
At the top of the item, six gray-shaded flat cardboard shapes are shown. Two are identical squares, each labeled '1 cm' on all four sides (top, bottom, left, and right). Four are identical horizontal rectangles, each labeled '2 cm' on the top and bottom sides and '1 cm' on the left and right sides.

The response options show line drawings of four 3D geometric solids with dashed lines representing hidden edges:
- Option A: A cube.
- Option B: A triangular prism resting on one of its rectangular faces.
- Option C: A truncated pyramid with a square or rectangular base and top.
- Option D: A tall right rectangular prism standing on a square base.
reference_items.calibration: Concurrent calibration of the TIMSS 2007 and 2011 fourth-grade mathematics data.

reference_items.subject: Mathematics
reference_items.stem:
Mr. Johnson asked the students in his school about their favorite subject.

This pie chart shows how many students liked each of 5 subjects.

[Image: Pie chart titled Favorite Subject, divided into various sizes and labeled with Math about one-third, Science about one-fourth, History about one-fifth, Gym less than one-fifth, and Music less than one-eighth.]

Which graph shows the same information as the pie chart?

options.label: A
options.text: [Image: Bar graph with y-axis labeled number of students and values from 0 to 25; x-axis with 5 columns, Math value of 30, Science value of 25, History value of 20, Gym value of 17, Music value of 8.]

options.label: B
options.text: [Image: Bar graph with y-axis labeled number of students and values from 0 to 25; x-axis with 5 columns, Math value of 30, Science value of 15, History value of 15, Gym value of 15, Music value of 14.]

options.label: C
options.text: [Image: Bar graph with y-axis labeled number of students and values from 0 to 25; x-axis with 5 columns, Math value of 20, Science value of 25, History value of 30, Gym value of 17, Music value of 8.]

options.label: D
options.text: [Image: Bar graph with y-axis labeled number of students and values from 0 to 25; x-axis with 5 columns, Math value of 25, Science value of 30, History value of 20, Gym value of 8, Music value of 12.]

reference_items.figure_description:
A pie chart titled "Favorite Subject" is divided into five sectors: Math (the largest sector, about one-third of the circle), Science (the second largest, about one-fourth of the circle), History (about one-fifth of the circle), Gym (smaller than History), and Music (the smallest sector, less than one-eighth of the circle). In order of sector size from largest to smallest: Math, Science, History, Gym, Music.

Each of the four response options shows a vertical bar graph with the vertical axis labeled "Number of Students" ranging from 0 to 35 with grid lines every 5 units, and the horizontal axis showing five subjects: Math, Science, History, Gym, Music.
- Graph A: Math = 30, Science = 25, History = 20, Gym = 17, Music = 8.
- Graph B: Math = 30, Science = 15, History = 15, Gym = 15, Music = 14.
- Graph C: Math = 20, Science = 25, History = 30, Gym = 17, Music = 8.
- Graph D: Math = 25, Science = 30, History = 20, Gym = 8, Music = 16.
reference_items.calibration: Concurrent calibration of the TIMSS 2007 and 2011 fourth-grade mathematics data.

slope.instructions: TIMSS scaled this 1-point item with the three-parameter logistic (3PL) model, which TIMSS uses for multiple-choice items, in the calibration "Concurrent calibration of the TIMSS 1995 and 2003 fourth-grade mathematics data". What is the item's slope (discrimination) parameter a? A higher a means that the item separates students of lower and higher mathematics ability more sharply. Choose the value closest to it. The state also lists reference items: the calibrated TIMSS items of the same grade most similar to this one (never the item itself or its other parts), most similar first, with their percent correct and their calibrated parameters, each on the scale of its own calibration. Use them to place this item.
